name: Alemet
title: Son of Becher, descendant of Benjamin
summary: Alemet is a person who appears in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:8, listed as one of the nine sons of Becher, son of Benjamin. He belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, known for its skilled warriors and military significance in Israel's early history. The lineage of Becher is described as very numerous; at a census, 20,200 fighting men were recorded (1 Chr 7:9). Beyond this entry in the genealogies, nothing more is told about Alemet's personal life or deeds. It is worth noting that the name Alemet also appears as a place name for a Levitical city in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 6:60), but the person and the place should not be confused.

keyEvents.title: Becher's descendants mustered as warriors
keyEvents.description: The descendants of Becher, including Alemet's line, were recorded as mighty warriors. At the muster, they numbered 20,200 men fit for war.

versions.summary: Alemet is a person mentioned in the Bible's genealogies. He appears as a descendant of Benjamin through Becher's line (1 Chronicles 7:8) and also as a Levitical city associated with the descendants of Aaron (1 Chronicles 6:60). As part of the tribe of Benjamin, he belongs to an important lineage in Israel's history.
versions.title: Descendant of Benjamin
versions.reason: [major] The summary conflates the person Alemet (son of Bekar) with the city of Alemet (a Levitical town). These are two distinct things – a person and a place name. The profile concerns the person, and the city should not be presented as if it were the same entity.; [major] The second key event element refers to the Levitical town of Alemet, not the person Alemet. This should either be removed or clearly marked as a footnote/additional information, not as a key event for the person.; [minor] The roles array is empty. Even for a genealogical figure, it should contain at least one role, e.g., 'Descendant of Benjamin' or 'Son of Bekar'.; [major] Alemet is listed among his own siblings. He should not appear in his own sibling list. 'Alemet' must be removed from the siblings array.; [minor] The fourth key event ('The significance of genealogies') is very general and does not specifically concern Alemet. It describes the entire genealogy in 1 Chronicles. This should either be tightened to focus more on Alemet, or removed.; [minor] The era 'united-kingdom' is reasonable if dating Bekar's line to this period, but it is uncertain. Since the person is primarily known from the genealogy in 1 Chronicles without further chronological detail, this is acceptable but uncertain.; [minor] Check that all sibling names are correct and in the proper format. In 1 Chron 7:8, nine sons of Bekar are mentioned: Semira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemet. When Alemet is removed from the list (since he is the person himself), eight siblings remain.

versions.summary: Alemet is a person mentioned in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7:8 as one of the sons of Becher, who was himself a son of Benjamin. He thus belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, a tribe that played an important role in Israel's history. Becher's lineage is described as numerous and warlike. The name Alemet also appears as the name of a Levitical city in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chron 6:60), but this is a place name and should not be confused with the person.
versions.title: Son of Becher, descendant of Benjamin
versions.reason: [minor] Alemet is mentioned in the genealogies in 1 Chronicles, but it is unclear whether he lived during the period of the united kingdom. The genealogies go back to the patriarchal era, and Bekar's generation (son of Benjamin, grandson of Jacob) places Alemet closer to the time of the patriarchs or the sojourn in Egypt. One could argue for 'patriarchs' or 'judges' as more appropriate. However, since it is uncertain and he is mentioned in the context of Chronicles, 'united-kingdom' can be defended. Keep unchanged but mark.; [minor] In the third footnote, 'etterksilistisk' appears, which is a typo for 'ettereksilsk' (or 'etter-eksilsk').; [major] According to 1 Chr 7:8, Bekar's sons are Semira, Joas, Elieser, Eljoenai, Omri, Jeremot, Abia, Anatot and Alemet. Thus there are eight brothers, and the list in siblings includes all eight others, but some of the names should be checked against ID conventions. 'semira' might possibly be 'zemira' (Hebrew: זמירה). Several Norwegian translations use the form 'Semira' or 'Zemira'.; [minor] The summary is good, and the reference to the Levitical city in 1 Chr 6:60 is a nice detail. It could be clarified that the city in Josh 21:18 is called Almon for consistency – this is already mentioned in the footnote, but the duplication in the summary is acceptable. Otherwise, the summary is informative and well phrased.

footnotes.text: The name Alemet (Hebrew: עַלְמֶת, 'Alemeth') may mean 'hide' or 'hiding place'. The same name is also used for a Levitical city in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chron 6:60), which in Joshua 21:18 is called Almon. It is uncertain whether the city was named after the person.

Becher, Alemet's father, is one of Benjamin's sons. According to 1 Chron 7:9, Becher's clan numbered 20,200 men fit for war at the muster, indicating a large and militarily significant clan in Israel.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles were likely compiled in the post-exilic period to document tribal inheritance rights and legitimize land distribution, priesthood, and temple service after the return from Babylon.

The tribe of Benjamin had its core area north of Jerusalem and played a central role in Israel's early history. The tribe was known for its skilled warriors, and several prominent biblical figures, including Saul and Paul, belonged to this tribe.

The names in Becher's lineage in 1 Chron 7:8 show interesting linguistic features. Several of the names, such as Anathoth and Alemet, are shared with well-known place names in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, which may indicate a connection between clans and the places where they settled.
